summary:
The Longer Catechism, a standard Russian Orthodox statement of the faith, teaches that faith and good works are inseparable, since faith without works is dead. On predestination it says that God has predestined to give all men, and has actually given them, preparatory grace and means sufficient for happiness. Citing the exposition of the Eastern patriarchs, it says that God foresaw that some would use their free will well and others ill, and predestined the former to glory while condemning the latter. The questions read do not say how a person is made right with God in the terms used in the Western debates over justification, or whether believers can fall away.

The Orthodox Confession of Peter Mogila teaches that a Christian must have right faith and good works to have eternal life; it quotes James that a man is justified by works and not by faith only, and that faith without works is dead. On predestination it distinguishes God's foreknowledge from his predestination: predestination follows foreknowledge and always determines good, never evil, since that would be contrary to God's goodness. The questions read do not say whether believers can fall away.

points.question: How do faith and works relate?
points.answer: A right faith in God and a life according to faith, with good works, go together; the catechism says a life according to faith and good works must be inseparable from faith because faith without works is dead.

points.question: Did God choose who would be saved?
points.answer: God's predestination of man to happiness remains unchanged; God has predestined to give all men preparatory grace and sufficient means. Citing the Eastern patriarchs, it says God foresaw who would use free will well or ill, and predestined the former to glory and condemned the latter.

points.question: How is a person made right with God?
points.answer: Right faith and good works together: whoever holds both has a certain hope of eternal salvation. Citing James 2:24, the confession says a man is justified by good works and not by faith only, and that faith without works is dead.

points.question: Did God choose who would be saved?
points.answer: Foreknowledge, predestination and providence differ in meaning. Predestination, joined with foreknowledge, determines only good and not evil, since appointing evil would be contrary to God's goodness; the order is foreknowledge, then predestination, then providence.

election.at: Longer Catechism, Q. 122-125; Orthodox Confession, Q. 30

excerpt.text: By good Works a Man is justified, and not by Faith only.

review.note: The Longer Catechism: Questions 4-5 and 120-125 read in the azbyka.ru English text on 2026-11-12. The catechism's longer treatment of faith, hope and the means of grace was not read, so justification and perseverance are left "not stated" rather than guessed. Not yet checked by a second reviewer. The Orthodox Confession: Question 1 and the opening of the question on foreknowledge and predestination read on 2026-11-12 in the azbyka.ru English text; the rest of that answer and the questions on grace and free will were not read. Matching the predestination answer to "offered to all" is our reading: the confession ties predestination to foreknowledge and rules out predestining to evil, but the part read does not say it is based on foreseen response. Date and endorsement are from general knowledge. Not yet checked by a second reviewer.
